Dodge Durango Owners Who Paid For Taillamp Repairs or Replacements Can Now File for Reimbursement
66 photos
Photo: Dodge
One of the most recognizable parts of the Durango can be found out back. Referred to as the racetrack taillamp by its maker, this full-width assembly is known to go dark a few LEDs at a time. Dodge finally made the reported problem its own, confirming that coverage on the rear lights now runs five years from the vehicle's in-service date. Unlimited miles, of course, but there's a catch.
The extension applies to certain 2018 through 2024 model year Durango sport utility vehicles, covering taillights that fail to illuminate or do so only partially. As it happens, the rear lighting units used by Dodge for those model years of the Durango may allow water to slip past the gaskets and seals. If that moisture pools where it has no business doing so, the LED circuit ultimately corrodes.
Given that diodes live on a sealed board, nobody in their right mind is willing to swap in a dead segment. The whole assembly has to go, and it's an expensive replacement. Dodge indirectly acknowledged the problem through a couple of technical service bulletins, namely TSBs from March 2020 and June 2021, meaning that Dodge is aware of the problem for at least six years now.
Owners and lessees have been paying close to $2,000 for replacement assemblies for many years now. For example, a December 2025 complaint filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration carries an $1,800 dealer quote (labor included). The five-year extension announced today pays some of that back.
Anyone who already covered such replacements out of pocket can file claims with Dodge using a dedicated website. Alternatively, customers and lessees can mail in the reimbursement form that comes with the customer notification letter. Reimbursements naturally require some documentation, so customers have to dig out appropriate proof of payment before trying to get their money back.
Photo: Dodge The website Dodge uses for Durango taillight claims is fcarecallreimbursement.com, and that's a bit curious. Is the Dodge brand using the same portal FCA US LLC, a.k.a. Stellantis North America, uses for recall refunds? It sure is, and it's now attached to a campaign that is not described as a recall even though partial or a lack of rear illumination increases the risk of a crash.
After some digging, yours truly discovered that a class action has been asking the courts for exactly what this warranty extension is not. Filed in the US District Court for the District of Delaware, the Cranstoun et al. v. FCA US LLC federal class-action lawsuit seeks either a court-ordered recall or full financial compensation for affected customers.
The class action covers 2014 through 2023 models, and one owner's complaint to the NHTSA describes a near-rear-end collision in 2019. Worse still, the same owner also described repeated police stops for their dead rear lights. Looking at the bigger picture, the Auburn Hills-based automaker may have decided on a customer satisfaction program because repairing it if the condition actually shows up is much cheaper than repairing potentially affected Durangos wholesale.
Matt McAlear, the chief executive officer of Dodge, frames the program as standing behind Durango owners. The racetrack taillights help the Durango stand out from other three-row people haulers, and McAlear credits customer feedback for this extension.
What now? If the rear lights work as intended in full, nothing. Only if segments go dark or glow faintly, then call your preferred dealer and let the extension handle the invoice. Durangos past the five-year window get six months of coverage from the notification date.
